rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 (Methodology) - the research is based on a documentary review of Jucar basin plans and allegations, media analysis, and participatory action research (six meetings/workshops with ARJ, CHJ, regional government, city council and NGOs, Table 1); Fig. 2 presents ARJ gauging data on water conveyed 1980-2022.
rows.notes: The study does not report its own result on drip irrigation reducing irrigation water consumption or enabling expansion of irrigated area. Its own material is documentary (how basin plans estimated and reallocated hypothetical savings) and participatory (stakeholder diagnosis and co-design of corrective measures). Fig. 2 (ARJ data) shows a decrease in diversions before modernisation and stabilisation at ~200 hm3 afterwards, and the text notes that the main pressurised pipeline (not plot-level drip) allowed demand to be met with 40% less water during the 2006-08 drought, but the study explicitly argues that reduced withdrawals are not real savings ('paper water', rebound effect) because return flows to the aquifer and wetland are lost; the per-hectare saving (3037 m3/ha/yr) is a CHJ planning estimate, not the study's own measurement, and the workshop could not validate that drip improves supply guarantee. The allocation of savings to new irrigable areas is documented only as a planning intention (1998/2014 PHJ) that was later redirected to wetland compensation; actual expansion elsewhere is cited from Ros et al. 2022. Hence the study is at best contrary to, or silent on, the claim as phrased.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 and Table 1 - documentary review of basin plans plus participatory action research with stakeholder workshops; Section 3.2 reports the workshop diagnosis and co-designed measures (Figs. 3-6).
rows.notes: The study does not measure or model aquifer recharge or groundwater levels itself. The reduction in aquifer recharge and return flows after drip adoption appears only as an effect identified by stakeholders in the participatory diagnosis (Fig. 3) and as something the 2015 basin plan acknowledged; the quantification of reduced return flows and recharge is attributed to cited work (Ruiz-Rodriguez 2017; Pool et al. 2021, 2022), and the study states that effects on wetland springs have not yet been quantified. Stakeholder perception of an impact is not the study's own evidence of the hydrological effect, so Q2 is no. The study does recommend piezometric monitoring, but as a future measure.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 - own documentary review and participatory action research (meetings and workshops, Table 1).
rows.notes: The study contains no data on plant height, harvest weight or crop yield under drip versus other systems; it is a water-policy and participatory-governance analysis of the ARJ-Albufera case. The only production-related remark is a cited estimate (Ruiz-Rodriguez et al. 2017) of increased farm income of about 800 EUR/ha, which is not the study's own result and not about plant growth. The citation appears misattributed (possibly confused with another Sanchis-Ibor et al. 2024 work).

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a qualitative policy/governance analysis (documentary review of Jucar basin plans plus participatory action research) with one figure of ARJ diversion data; it provides no agronomic or hydrological measurements of its own, and its central argument is that drip 'savings' in planning were unproven paper water with rebound and wetland impacts.
